1.pericope_label: Then all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in the room of his father Amaziah. He built Eloth, and restored it to Judah, after that the king slept with his fathers.

schools.summary: Ellicott argues that Uzziah and Azariah are both genuine names rather than an abbreviation or a copyist's blunder, noting that this writer uses the first almost always and Kings both, that the Greek of Kings levels its usage to the second, and that the Assyrian inscriptions of Tiglathpileser use the longer form uniformly, so that the king was known by both but to foreigners chiefly by the second; he also identifies the port as the Idumean harbour on the Red Sea and observes that the first four verses are identical with the parallel.
Gill passes the opening verses over to the parallel account, where the same king appears under the other name.

Clarke reads the accession clause to mean that the people all agreed to place this son on his father's throne, notes that the king is called by several different names, and sets out the whole course of the reign in advance, from the piety and prosperity under the prophet to the campaigns, the building, the elation, the leprosy and the burial.

debates: Whether the two names of this king are both genuine, which Ellicott maintains against Schrader and others who make the shorter form a popular abbreviation or a transcriber's blunder.
How much of the opening is proper to this book at all, where Ellicott observes that the first four verses are identical with the parallel in Kings.
What the fortifying of the port at the outset signified, which Ellicott takes as the act completing the subjugation of Edom that the previous reign had begun.
outliers: Ellicott brings the Assyrian inscriptions to bear on the question of the name, the king appearing there uniformly under the longer form.
themes: Then all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in the room of his father Amaziah.
He built Eloth, and restored it to Judah, after that the king slept with his fathers.

5.pericope_label: And he sought God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God: and as long as he sought the Lord, God made him to prosper. And he went forth and warred against the Philistines, and brake down the wall of Gath, and the wall of Jabneh, and the wall of Ashdod, and built cities about Ashdod, and among the Philistines. And God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians that dwelt in Gur–baal, and the Mehunims. And the Ammonites gave gifts to Uzziah: and his name spread abroad even to the entering in of Egypt; for he strengthened himself exceedingly.

schools.summary: Ellicott will not keep the received text of the prophet's character, preferring the reading of some Hebrew manuscripts and of the Greek, Syriac, Arabic and Targum which gives the fear of God rather than the visions of God, as Rashi and Kimchi had suggested, and draws from the relation that Zechariah was the king's counsellor in the political as well as the religious sphere, the distinction between the two being then unknown; he notices that the two histories substitute different judgments at this point, identifies Jabneh and Ashdod and judges the Philistines reduced to vassalage without annexation, and leaves Gur-Baal unidentified.

Gill clears away two candidates for the prophet before suggesting a son of the Zechariah whom Joash slew, supplies the Philistine grievance from the reign of Jehoram, reports the Targum making it the Word of the Lord that helped the king, and allows that the Ammonites may have been merely desirous of friendship.

Clarke builds on the received reading, taking the visions of God for the true interpretation of divine prophecies and inferring that the prophet was the young king's tutor, quotes the same Targum at greater length with the Arabians of Gerar and the plains of Meun, and makes the Ammonite gifts an annual tribute.

debates: Whether the prophet's character should read the visions of God or the fear of God, where Ellicott emends with the versions and Rashi and Kimchi, and Clarke builds his whole account of the man on the received text.

Who the Zechariah of this verse was, which Ellicott leaves as an otherwise unknown prophet, Gill makes perhaps a son of the Zechariah whom Joash slew, and Clarke guesses to have been the king's tutor.
Where Gur-Baal lay, which Ellicott says is mentioned only here and is unknown, the Targum making it Gerar and the Greek apparently Petra, with Gedor-Baal proposed.
outliers: Ellicott observes that where this writer accounts for the king's prosperity by his seeking God, Kings at the same point makes its usual deduction that the high places were not taken away.
themes: And he sought God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God: and as long as he sought the Lord, God made him to prosper.
And he went forth and warred against the Philistines, and brake down the wall of Gath, and the wall of Jabneh, and the wall of Ashdod, and built cities about Ashdod, and among the Philistines.
And God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians that dwelt in Gur–baal, and the Mehunims.
And the Ammonites gave gifts to Uzziah: and his name spread abroad even to the entering in of Egypt; for he strengthened himself exceedingly.

9.pericope_label: Moreover Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the corner gate, and at the valley gate, and at the turning of the wall, and fortified them. Also he built towers in the desert, and digged many wells: for he had much cattle, both in the low country, and in the plains: husbandmen also, and vine dressers in the mountains, and in Carmel: for he loved husbandry. Moreover Uzziah had an host of fighting men, that went out to war by bands, according to the number of their account by the hand of Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the ruler, under the hand of Hananiah, one of the king’s captains. The whole number of the chief of the fathers of the mighty men of valour were two thousand and six hundred. And under their hand was an army, three hundred thousand and seven thousand and five hundred, that made war with mighty power, to help the king against the enemy. And Uzziah prepared for them throughout all the host shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones. And he made in Jerusalem engines, invented by cunning men, to be on the towers and upon the bulwarks, to shoot arrows and great stones withal. And his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong.

schools.summary: Ellicott places the three towers at the exposed points of the capital, corrects the English margin on the fortifying, reads the desert as the grazing country west of the Dead Sea and the wells as hewn cisterns, takes Carmel for the fruitful field rather than a place, renders the closing clause as a lover of the soil, and describes the muster administratively, the host in organised troops with each chief over about a hundred and twenty men and the equipment divided between heavy and light armed.

Gill supplies the history of the broken corner gate, puts the desert towers in Arabia for the protection of travellers and shepherds, identifies the twenty-six hundred as the commanders and reckons the army larger than the previous reign's by seven thousand five hundred, and canvasses the rival claimants to the invention of the engines before settling it on skilful men among the Jews in this reign.

Clarke makes the country towers a defence for flocks and shepherds, takes Carmel for a place-name and reports two of them from Calmet, turns the love of husbandry into a political maxim that no state can prosper without agriculture since the king himself is served by the field, reads the armoury as weapons held ready for the subjects' hands, and claims the engines as the first warlike machines on record, long prior to Greece or Rome, supporting it from the length of sieges before them.

debates: Whether Carmel here is a place or a common noun, where Clarke reports two Carmels from Calmet and Ellicott reads the fruitful field or glebe land.

Who invented the siege engines, where Gill weighs the Greeks, the Romans, the Syrians and Phoenicians on Pliny's authority and the Carthaginians before deciding for Judea in this reign, and Clarke independently calls this the first such engine on record.

What the towers in the open country were for: the protection of travellers and shepherds (Gill), the defence of flocks and husbandmen (Clarke), or a guard for the royal herds in the grazing country (Ellicott).
outliers: Clarke spends his longest note of the chapter on husbandry as a perfection in a king, holding that where a king encourages it the people cannot be reduced to wretchedness even should trade fail, because there is plenty of bread.
Gill cites Diodorus Siculus for the claim that siege engines had not been found out when Nineveh was besieged.
themes: Moreover Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the corner gate, and at the valley gate, and at the turning of the wall, and fortified them.

Also he built towers in the desert, and digged many wells: for he had much cattle, both in the low country, and in the plains: husbandmen also, and vine dressers in the mountains, and in Carmel: for he loved husbandry.

Moreover Uzziah had an host of fighting men, that went out to war by bands, according to the number of their account by the hand of Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the ruler, under the hand of Hananiah, one of the king’s captains.
The whole number of the chief of the fathers of the mighty men of valour were two thousand and six hundred.

16.pericope_label: But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the Lord his God, and went into the temple of the Lord to burn incense upon the altar of incense. And Azariah the priest went in after him, and with him fourscore priests of the Lord, that were valiant men: And they withstood Uzziah the king, and said unto him, It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the Lord, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed; neither shall it be for thine honour from the Lord God. Then Uzziah was wroth, and had a censer in his hand to burn incense: and while he was wroth with the priests, the leprosy even rose up in his forehead before the priests in the house of the Lord, from beside the incense altar. And Azariah the chief priest, and all the priests, looked upon him, and, behold, he was leprous in his forehead, and they thrust him out from thence; yea, himself hasted also to go out, because the Lord had smitten him. And Uzziah the king was a leper unto the day of his death, and dwelt in a several house, being a leper; for he was cut off from the house of the Lord: and Jotham his son was over the king’s house, judging the people of the land. Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, first and last, did Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, write. So Uzziah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the field of the burial which belonged to the kings; for they said, He is a leper: and Jotham his son reigned in his stead.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the king to have wanted the pontificate as well as the crown, on the model of the Egyptian rulers, and denies that he was merely reviving a precedent of David and Solomon since it can hardly be proved those kings ever performed priestly functions; he renders the thrusting out as hurrying him away and the hasting as that he thrust himself, reports Thenius's reservation that the chronicler followed traditional exegesis in making the leprosy a judgment, relays the embellishment in Josephus, and renders the several house as the hospital or lazar house with the reason for it this writer's own addition.

Gill supplies the strength that lifted the king up, has the high priest go in after him to hinder him and the priests surround him so that he could not approach the altar, observes that the leprosy appeared in the forehead where all could see, and dates the death to the same year as the stroke on one chronologer's reckoning.

Clarke makes the separation total, from all society domestic, civil and religious, has the son become regent because the father could no longer discharge the office, records that the history Isaiah wrote of this king is totally lost, and explains the burial outside the royal sepulchres by the supposition that even a place of burial would be defiled by a leper's body; Wesley denies that the priests used any force, fixes the stroke as coming from beside the altar by an invisible hand, and finds the punishment answering the sin as face answers face in a glass.

debates: Whether the priests restrained the king physically, where Gill has them surround him so that he could not approach the altar while Wesley denies any laying on of hands, since the censer is still in his hand in the next verse, and Ellicott's renderings of hurrying him out and of his thrusting himself away support Wesley.
What the king was attempting, which Ellicott makes a bid for the pontificate on the Egyptian model against the view that he was reviving a precedent of David and Solomon.
Whether the leprosy is to be read as a judgment on the offence, which Thenius ascribes to the chronicler's traditional exegesis while granting the invasion of the sanctuary itself historical.
outliers: Ellicott relays the embellishment in Josephus, that the great earthquake the prophet mentions fell as the king threatened the priests and that a ray of sunlight through the cloven roof produced the disease.

Wesley reads the sentence as exactly reciprocal, the king thrust out of the courts open to the meanest subject because he thrust himself into the place reserved for priests, and losing a dignity he held by right because he invaded one he did not.
